newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Q3 borrowing needs lowest in decades.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Q3 borrowing needs lowest in decades.

text.p: Strong economic momentum will reduce the government's third-quarter borrowing requirements to the lowest for that period in decades, the Treasury Department said on Monday.

Treasury said its net market borrowing in the July-September third quarter would be $10 billion. A department official said the last time third-quarter borrowing was comparably low was in the late 1970s when it borrowed $10.4 billion in the third quarter of 1979 and $10.8 billion in the third quarter of 1978.
A steadily expanding economy and a booming stock market have generated much stronger tax revenues for the government than it anticipated.

In the second quarter, which ended June 30, Treasury actually paid down the government debt by $71.5 billion. The second quarter typically produces more revenues since it includes the April 15 deadline for filing individual income tax returns for the prior year.
Treasury had earlier forecast a smaller second-quarter paydown of $65 billion but said "a surge in receipts" helped shrink the debt more sharply.
Economist Lou Crandall of R.H. Wrightson and Associates Inc in New York said the estimate for third-quarter borrowing was "considerably lower" than most private analysts had expected.
He added that it implied a lower budget deficit in the 1997 fiscal year ending Sept 30 than has been widely forecast and a better chance of achieving a balanced budget next year.

"It's consistent with a budget deficit of $30 billion or less for this year," Crandall said, adding, "The lower the deficit is this year, the more likely the improvement is to continue over into the early part of next year."

The Clinton administration and Congress are negotiating a budget and tax deal that aims to balance the budget by 2002 or before, and to restructure several health care programs, including taking $115 billion from the Medicare program for senior citizens.

Crandall said credit for progress in shrinking the deficit goes to the durable economic expansion since the 1990-1991 recession and suggested that a balance between income and spending might come sooner if there was no budget deal.

The risk is that a budget pact "will salvage the red ink at the last moment" through tax cuts and spending, Crandall said. He suggested the political effort would be better directed in grappling with structural deficit problems further in the future when an aging Baby Boom population increases the demand for government programs early in the next century.
